title: Tarwen of the Silver Star
type: NPC · Silver Star emissary, historical custodian and former warrior
dek: A host and former warrior whose defense of Zarathian tradition makes room for careful listening, unanswered questions and a distinction between accusation and judgment.

facts.Later work: Evidence, property and care for new arrivals
facts.Personal account: Former warrior; age and injuries changed his work

body:
Tarwen introduces himself as an emissary of the Order of the Silver Stars. He guides newcomers through Fein Uaill, explains his society’s convictions and appears in its councils and gatherings. His courtesy can make room for an awkward guest; it also has a sharp boundary when a guest declares service to the gods.

A castle offered to newcomers

Tarwen welcomes Elenia, Adelia, Draygar, Krone and Olokun to an old castle among wheat fields and vineyards. When Draygar questions whether it is really theirs, Tarwen confirms the gift and presents it as an example of mortal generosity. He says servant mages can take them by teleportation circle to Zarathis, and leaves them time to speak privately.

His account of ascension

Asked by Elenia how ascension works, Tarwen urges daily improvement and cooperation, so mortals rather than gods become masters of creation. These are his convictions and his account of the society, rather than proof of what every resident believes. On returning, he offers to show the company the proving grounds, where he says warriors gain stature. His welcome establishes a guide’s role; it does not establish his rank, ancestry or authority over all Fein Uaill.

The city he shows the newcomers

Tarwen offers to show the visiting company the land after introducing the Silver Star through structure, honor and respect for the past. On the shore he names the city the Gates of Aelthor, after the first king following the breaking of the world. His explanation supplies a local name and remembered history, not a complete account of that catastrophe.

The tour continues through teleportation circles and waiting mages to the country house offered to the company. Tarwen confirms the gift when Draygar doubts it and says further needs can be brought to the servant mages. The port and coast are part of a lived network of places, hosts and expectations, rather than an isolated arrival scene.

Where the welcome meets allegiance

When Adelia names Moirah and acknowledges serving her, Tarwen tells her the land’s bounty is closed to her. He presents opposition to the gods as a condition of belonging. Olokun asks for patience with people who have come from another land, and Elenia asks to speak to Adelia privately.

Tarwen allows the private conversation and continues the journey to the offered home. The scene holds his generosity beside his intolerance of divine allegiance. It does not supply a complete legal ruling on Adelia’s future residence, or show that every resident of Fein Uaill acts on his convictions in the same way.

Later, when Draygar describes his work, Tarwen again invites him toward the order’s arcane craftsmanship. He does not chastise him for attending to his forge first: he says time matters, but so does care, and that he trusts discerning judgment. His stated ideal of order includes personal discretion as well as exclusion.

Wren, the waltz and a changed profession

Olokun brings Wren to Tarwen at a gathering. Offered a choice of dance, she admits unfamiliarity; Tarwen chooses a waltz and leads without treating her embarrassment as a failure. He says he was a warrior when young, before age and injuries made him change his field of expertise.

The account of his past remains his own. It gives context for his practiced dancing without establishing the dates, battles or injuries of an otherwise unrecovered military career. His interest in Wren is specific: Elenia has praised her, and he wants to hear the battle through her eyes as well as through Aria’s and Elenia’s.

When Wren insists on her companions’ shared contribution, he keeps the invitation open. They part expecting another conversation. The warmth of the exchange remains beside the harder welcome he gave Adelia; neither scene requires Tarwen to become the same kind of host to everyone.

A voice at the war council

At the war council, Tarwen argues that finding the island where the greater war is being fought should take priority. He also asks why Aria’s concern about Death’s intervention has changed. He participates in the discussion rather than appearing only as a ceremonial guide.

When Scribonia urges the company to treat gods as individuals and attempt peace, Tarwen answers from what he says underlies their nation: mortals can rise above the gods, and the old stories remember divine greed and cruelty. These are his political and historical convictions. The exchange does not independently prove every story he cites or make his words the final judgment of the whole council.

Listening without surrendering his judgment

Tarwen’s interest in Wren continues beyond the dance. In their later conversation he makes time after a meeting and offers a guard tower for privacy. He dislikes gossip, but insists that running a place well requires listening. He can hear a story without accepting every conclusion its teller draws.

He describes the Silver Star as shepherds of history, preserving the finished work while the Flame forges new events. Yet if disaster threatens Zarathis, he says his duty as a citizen comes before duty to the order. Loyalty to the institution is not the only obligation he can name.

His welcome still has a boundary: he will hear much short of heresy or insurrection, and he warns that listening may leave him unconvinced. Wren has gained an attentive interlocutor, not a promise that he will adopt her view.

At the earlier gathering, his toast to Narissa had made historical memory personal. He praises the mother’s care for Magnus and loyalty to Aria, then asks Magnus to remember how he was raised. Commemoration is also an expectation placed on the living.

An old warrior’s unanswered question

When Magnus later seeks help, Tarwen distinguishes what he can offer from what belongs to the Verdant Circle. He will not grant access that another institution controls. Respect for boundaries is part of how he understands historical duty, rather than evidence that his own authority covers the whole island.

He calls service voluntary and treats the Silver Star as a keeper of communal memory. He is willing to leave innovation to those better suited to it, while admitting that revolutions sometimes have to happen.

A proposal to avoid risking lives gives him pause. He calls the immediate goal noble, yet wonders what happens to heroism, bravery and the way ancestors understood life if danger is removed. He explicitly has no settled answer about the long consequences. The former warrior’s uncertainty gives his traditionalism a question to work on, not a complete rejection of saving lives.

Care, evidence and a member’s property

In the Month of War, Year 3, Eldin brings Tarwen disturbing news about Magnus. Tarwen asks what actually happened instead of accepting an impersonal report that someone has returned to life. The possibility of a man arranging the same act he condemned in someone else troubles him.

He says he will arrange protection and shut the relevant teleportation circles. But when the discussion turns to consequences for Magnus’s property and title, he insists on proof and formal charges. Concern does not itself transfer ownership: until the accusations are established, he says the property remains Magnus’s.

Tarwen offers the Silver Star as a trusted custodian and describes caring for and questioning newly arrived people before asking Eldin to help identify them. He then leaves to assist the captain. His later work joins caution with practical care, without establishing every promised security measure or a final judgment against Magnus.

His exact rank, ancestry, full former military service and eventual fate remain unresolved.
